name: Disorder of Urea Cycle Metabolism and Ammonia Detoxification
aliases: Hyperammonemia due to Urea Cycle Defect

criteria.description: Elevated blood ammonia levels above normal reference range
Deficiency or dysfunction of one or more urea cycle enzymes confirmed by biochemical or genetic testing
Clinical signs consistent with ammonia intoxication such as vomiting, lethargy, and altered mental status
Increased urinary orotic acid excretion in certain enzyme defects (e.g., OTC deficiency)
Identification of pathogenic variants in genes encoding urea cycle enzymes

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of hyperammonemia with enzyme deficiency or pathogenic genetic variant plus compatible clinical presentation
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis may require exclusion of other causes of hyperammonemia.

pathognomonic.notes: Rapid onset of neurological deterioration due to ammonia toxicity
searchTerms: severe brain dysfunction from high ammonia

pathognomonic.notes: Biochemical hallmark of urea cycle disorders

pathognomonic.symptomName: Cerebral edema secondary to ammonia accumulation
pathognomonic.notes: Can lead to increased intracranial pressure and coma

common.notes: Common early symptom during hyperammonemic crises
Behavioral manifestation in infants and children

occasional.notes: May occur during acute metabolic decompensation
Impaired coordination due to neurological damage
Reduced muscle tone during acute episodes
Avoidance of protein-rich foods due to intolerance

laboratory: Increased glutamine levels in plasma and CSF
Elevated urinary orotic acid (in OTC deficiency)
Low plasma citrulline or arginine depending on enzyme defect
imaging: MRI brain showing cerebral edema during acute crises
White matter abnormalities in chronic cases
genetic: Pathogenic variants in genes encoding urea cycle enzymes (e.g., OTC, CPS1, ASS1, ASL, ARG1)
other: Enzyme activity assays in liver or fibroblasts

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of metabolic acidosis with elevated anion gap
Different enzyme defects affecting amino acid metabolism
Hyperammonemia secondary to liver dysfunction rather than enzyme defect

redFlags: Rapidly progressive encephalopathy with vomiting and lethargy
Markedly elevated plasma ammonia without liver disease
Recurrent episodes of hyperammonemia triggered by protein intake or catabolic stress
references: Summar ML, et al. Urea Cycle Disorders Overview. GeneReviews. 2021.
Häberle J, et al. Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2012.
Brusilow SW, Maestri NE. Urea cycle disorders: diagnosis, pathophysiology, and therapy. Adv Pediatr. 1996.
